title: Children and builders (Berakhot 64a)
hookLine: the rabbis read banayich, your children, as bonayich, your builders
last: TO KNOW IS TO BE CLOSE.

lines: A KID, A TOWER OF BLOCKS.
cards: On a living-room rug, a kid is stacking blocks. Red on blue, a yellow one balanced on top, a tower that leans and somehow holds. An adult walks past and sees a mess to tidy before dinner.
The kid sees a city. Who's right? The Talmud has an answer, and it hides in a single vowel.
Near the close of Berakhot, the tractate of blessings, a rabbi quotes Isaiah's verse about children and reads one word of it a second way. Same letters, different sound.

teach.b: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And all thy children shall be taught of the LORD; And great shall be the peace of thy children." Turn it four ways. First, the word.
Thy children, in Hebrew, is banayich: ben, a son, a child, with the ending that means yours. Second, the move.
In Berakhot, Rabbi Elazar, in the name of Rabbi Chanina, says that students of the wise increase peace in the world, and quotes this verse. Then he adds: don't read banayich, your children.
Read bonayich, your builders. Without vowel marks, the way it stands in a scroll, the two look alike. Only the sound changes.
Third, the kind of move. The rabbis call it al tikri, don't read. It doesn't erase the plain meaning; Isaiah still says children.

teach.h: AL TIKRI: A SECOND READING BESIDE.
teach.b: The second reading stands beside the first, like a harmony over a melody: your children will be taught, and your builders will have great peace. Fourth, who the builders are. In the passage, they're the ones who learn.
A child taught today is already laying stones for a peace not yet built.
Back to the rug. The adult sees a mess. The Talmud, reading Isaiah, sees a builder learning how a thing holds, and that learning, says Berakhot, is how peace gets built.

how: The passage from the end of tractate Berakhot, with its reading of banayich as bonayich, is printed in some prayer books and is quoted at some celebrations of learning, such as the completion of a tractate.

o: a proverb that parents build their children's future
a Talmud reading where your children become your builders
a law that children must help build the synagogue

games.q: children and builders — tap the pairs.

s: the rabbis changed the letters of Isaiah's verse
the letters stay the same; only the vowels are read differently.
in Berakhot, students of the wise increase peace in the world
Rabbi Elazar says it in the name of Rabbi Chanina, and quotes Isaiah.
a second reading erases the verse's plain meaning
al tikri lays a second meaning beside the first; Isaiah still says children.

games.q: you're a rabbi reading Isaiah: "great shall be the peace of thy children." the word for children catches your eye. what do you do?
o: read the same letters a second way: your builders.
games.why: don't read banayich, read bonayich. the children are the builders, and the learners build the peace.

practice: Bring one child to mind: your own, a niece, a student, a kid down the street, or, if no child comes, the child you once were.
Picture them building something, a tower, a drawing, a question they keep asking, and see the thing they made rather than the mess around it.
Find one sentence of encouragement about the building, not about being good, and if you pray, hold their name in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Children and builders. Banayich and bonayich: one set of letters in Isaiah, read two ways in the Talmud, so that the children are the builders. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, without vowel marks: the same letters read as your children or your builders.

carryVoice: Your line: children are builders. Same letters, two readings, both standing at once. Same time tomorrow.
